passages.text: Highly Attenuated Poxvirus-Based Vaccines Against Emerging Viral Diseases
Graphical abstract

Although one member of the poxvirus family, variola virus, has caused one of the most devastating human infections worldwide, smallpox, the knowledge gained over the last 30 years on the molecular, virological and immunological mechanisms of these viruses has allowed the use of members of this family as vectors for the generation of recombinant vaccines against numerous pathogens. In this review, we cover different aspects of the history and biology of poxviruses with emphasis on their application as vaccines, from first- to fourth-generation, against smallpox, monkeypox, emerging viral diseases highlighted by the World Health Organization (COVID-19, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, Ebola and Marburg virus diseases, Lassa fever, Middle East respiratory syndrome and severe acute respiratory syndrome, Nipah and other henipaviral diseases, Rift Valley fever and Zika), as well as against one of the most concerning prevalent virus, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome. We discuss the implications in human health of the 2022 monkeypox epidemic affecting many countries, and the rapid prophylactic and therapeutic measures adopted to control virus dissemination within the human population. We also describe the preclinical and clinical evaluation of the Modified Vaccinia virus Ankara and New York vaccinia virus poxviral strains expressing heterologous antigens from the viral diseases listed above. Finally, we report different approaches to improve the immunogenicity and efficacy of poxvirus-based vaccine candidates, such as deletion of immunomodulatory genes, insertion of host-range genes and enhanced transcription of foreign genes through modified viral promoters. Some future prospects are also highlighted.
Introduction

The Poxviridae family includes a group of enveloped double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) viruses with a brick-shape structure, a size of 200-400 nm and genomes ranging from 130 to 375 kb that infect a wide variety of hosts, including mammals, birds, marsupials, reptiles, fish and insects. According to the last International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) Master Species List (2021.v3), the Poxviridae family comprises two subfamilies (Entomopoxvirinae and Chordopoxvirinae) and is subdivided into 22 genera (https://ictv.global). The orthopoxviruses (OPXVs) are the most widely studied genus among poxviruses due to their significant pathogenicity in humans. In particular, this genus is widely known for variola virus (VARV), the causal agent of smallpox, vaccinia virus (VACV), used as vaccine for smallpox eradication and the most representative member for molecular and cellular studies, or cowpox (CPXV) and monkeypox (MPXV) viruses, which persistently infect wild and domestic animals causing zoonotic outbreaks in humans that pose a serious threat to public health. OPXV genus also includes other viruses such as raccoonpox, taterapox, camelpox, volepox, ectromelia, Abatino macacapox, skunkpox and Akhmeta.

Poxvirus genomes can encode more than 200 proteins and around 100 of them are incorporated within virions. Essential viral functions are grouped in the central region of the genome and are conserved throughout the family. In contrast, species-specific genes required for virulence and host infection and immunomodulatory genes lie near the termini.

Replication of poxviruses occurs entirely in the cytoplasm of the infected cell. Virions enter cells by direct fusion of viral and cellular membranes or by macropinocytosis and subsequent release from an endosomal compartment. After entry, the lateral bodies are disassembled, while the core remains intact and is transported by the cellular microtubule network to a perinuclear region where it undergoes morphological changes to be activated at the early transcription site. Messenger RNAs produced by the viral DNA-dependent RNA-polymerase, which encode early proteins, are released from the core into the cytoplasm where translation on cellular polysomes occurs. After early gene expression and a complex and poorly understood uncoating process, the core wall disintegrates and the DNA genome is released, being immediately associated with membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum and several early viral proteins to constitute a prereplication center. As DNA synthesis progresses, prereplication foci expand leading to the formation of viral replication factories. Following DNA replication and intermediate and late gene expression, the viral genome is encapsulated to constitute immature virions (IV), that in turn mature into intracellular mature virus (MV), which represents the first viral infectious form. MV can be released after cell lysis or can acquire a second lipid bilayer membrane from trans-Golgi network to form wrapped virions (WV) (also known as intracellular enveloped virions) and bud off as extracellular enveloped virions (EV).

Upon infection poxviruses induce Toll-like receptor (TLR)-independent and dependent innate signalling pathways. Multiple host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including cytosolic DNA sensors, RNA sensors, various TLRs and inflammasome components, have been involved in the recognition of poxviruses. They are involved in the triggering of signalling cascades, the activation of transcription factors and, finally, the expression of antiviral effectors. To prevent the host immune defense poxviruses encode a wide range of immunomodulatory proteins that evade or disrupt host antiviral responses induced by PRRs. These interactions determine the outcome of poxvirus infection. Over the past few decades, the study of poxvirus-sensing and virus-host protein interactions has provided fundamental insights that have led to translational applications for the development of safer and more effective attenuated poxvirus-based vaccine candidates.

In this study we review the history and evolution of poxvirus-based vaccines against smallpox, highlighting the main strategies that have been used to optimize the safety and immunogenicity of attenuated poxvirus strains. We also describe the 2022 monkeypox (MPOX) epidemic and measures adopted for its control, as well as the contribution of attenuated poxvirus-based recombinant viruses as vaccine candidates against emerging viral diseases with pandemic potential [coronavirus disease (COVID-19), Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola and Marburg virus diseases, Lassa fever, Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), Nipah and other henipaviral diseases, Rift Valley fever and Zika], and against one of the most concerning prevalent viruses, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV-1), the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
Poxvirus-Based Vaccines: From Variolation to Fourth-Generation Vaccines
Variolation and first-generation vaccines

Smallpox is one of the most devastating and widespread diseases known to humanity and, at the same time, the only human disease that has been declared eradicated in the world. This achievement is considered one of the most relevant milestones in global public health and was made possible by the use of vaccines.

Since the 15th century people worldwide have attempted to prevent smallpox by intentionally exposing healthy people to small amounts of infectious material from smallpox sores, a practice known as variolation. However, eventually, the British country doctor Edward Jenner was recognized with introducing smallpox vaccination to England in 1796. He harvested material from the lesions of a milkmaid who had acquired the infection from cattle and inoculated a child with this material to protect him against VARV. Subsequently, Jenner challenged the boy with smallpox-derived material by scarification and succeeded in preventing him from developing the disease. After additional investigations Jenner published his research marking the onset of the vaccination era.

In the years following Jenner's discovery different seed viruses used for vaccination were distributed worldwide while being repetitively passaged in humans and amplified in animals. The most common VACV strains used to manufacture the first-generation smallpox vaccines include the New York City Board of Health (NYCBH), used for the production of Dryvax  and EM-63 vaccines, and Lister, used for the production of Elstree and Lancy-Vaxina Berna vaccines. Other VACV strains widely used in Europe, China or the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) were Ankara, Copenhagen, Bern, TianTan and Tashkent. They were administered percutaneously by skin scarification, which produced a cutaneous reaction as a result of local virus replication. In naive individuals, vaccination correlated with the development of neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) against VACV as well as with specific CD4 and CD8 T cells. Both responses persist for many decades and correlate with protection against smallpox and other related OPXVs. Thanks to the combined efforts of the World Health Organization (WHO), national health agencies and scientific community worldwide, smallpox was eradicated from South America in 1971, Asia in 1975 and Africa in 1977, and WHO declared worldwide eradication in 1980.
Second-generation vaccines

Although the first-generation vaccines employed during the smallpox eradication campaign were considered safe compared to the possibility of contracting smallpox, a significant number of serious adverse effects ranging from mild (e.g., mild rash, malaise and fever) to severe (e.g., eczema vaccinatum, progressive vaccinia and post-vaccinial encephalitis) were reported. These findings promoted the development of second-generation vaccines produced in tissue cultures.

Lister was the first VACV strain used for the generation of cell-cultured-derived smallpox vaccines and was passaged in rabbit kidney cells to produce RIVM vaccine or in primary cells derived from chicken embryos to produce Lister and Elstree-Bavarian-Nordic (BN) vaccines. Other second-generation VACV-based vaccines were produced using NYCBH grown in normal diploid MRC-5 human lung cells or in Vero cells. These include CCSV (cell-cultured smallpox vaccine), ACAM2000 and CJ-50300 vaccines. ACAM2000 vaccine, derived from a clone isolated from Dryvax , is a replication-competent smallpox vaccine licensed by the USA Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for people at high risk for smallpox infection. In USA, ACAM2000 is only available through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for the prevention of MPOX under an Expanded Access Investigational New Drug application.

Considerable animal and limited human data suggest that second-generation smallpox vaccines have immunogenicity and efficacy profiles similar to their parental strains. However, they also maintain the risk of serious adverse events, particularly in individuals with eczema, immunodeficiency, and other specific conditions. Consequently, third-generation vaccines were developed to produce highly attenuated or non-replicating VACV strains, while maintaining immunogenicity and protective efficacy.
Third-generation vaccines

Vaccines from this third-generation were mainly produced by classical attenuation after multiple passages of the parental VACV strains in alternative tissue culture cells. During this process, a large number of deletions and random mutations were introduced into the virus genome resulting in attenuated VACV strains mostly unable to replicate in human cells. Among them we can highlight the well-known Lister clone 16 m8 (LC16m8), Modified Vaccinia virus Ankara (MVA) and Dairen I strain (DIs), as well as the most recent KVAC103 vaccine.

LC16m8 is an attenuated, replicating smallpox vaccine derived from the Lister strain of VACV developed in Japan in 1975. LC16m8 was tested in more than 100,000 infants in Japan in the early 1970's without serious adverse events, but it was not tested against smallpox since vaccination campaign was discontinued in 1976. Its attenuated phenotype is due to a single-nucleotide deletion in the VACV B5R gene,, which produces an inefficient release of EVs.. B5 is highly immunogenic and induces both humoral and cellular immune responses, so there were some concerns about the immunogenicity and efficacy of LC16m8. Nevertheless, some studies performed in different immunodeficient mouse models confirmed an extremely low virulence of LC16m8 and the induction of protective immunity after a challenge with the wild-type Western Reserve (WR) strain compared to the parental Lister strain. The LC16m8 vaccine was later modified through elimination of the entire B5R gene to avoid reversion.

MVA is one of the most commonly used third-generation vaccines. It derives from the Chorioallantois Vaccinia virus Ankara (CVA) strain after 572 serial passages in chicken embryo fibroblast (CEF) cells. After testing in clinical trials,, MVA was administered to more than 120,000 individuals in Germany in 1977 without any documented severe adverse event. During its generation, MVA lost around 30 kb of the parental CVA genome, most of them located in both left and right terminal regions, and mainly involved in virus-host interaction and evasion of the host immune response. These extensive gene deletions also resulted in a restriction of the ability of MVA to replicate in almost all mammalian cells, including human cells. However, MVA undergoes viral DNA replication and expresses early, intermediate and late viral proteins, although it cannot form MVs. Some of the best-known VACV host-range genes, such as C7L, K3L, E3L, F1L and B18R, and immunomodulatory genes, such as B16R, C12L, A41L, C6L, K7R and A46R, are still functional in the MVA genome (referred to the genomic nomenclature used for VACV strain Copenhagen, since this nomenclature is widely used). Although MVA has not been directly evaluated in humans for efficacy against VARV, several clinical trials have demonstrated its safety and immunogenicity profiles. Moreover, MVA has been tested against other OPXVs, such as MPXV, triggering protection. Hence, MVA is considered the "gold standard" for VACV vaccines and is also a very promising vaccine vector against different infectious diseases, such as AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, Ebola, Zika, Chikungunya and West Nile fever, and cancer, among others.

Dairen I strain (DIs) is a host-range restrictive mutant of dermovaccinia virus strain DIE obtained after 13 serial passages in 1-day-old eggs. Homologous recombination between two highly similar 16 bp-sequences in DIE strain resulted in a 15.4 kb deletion containing 19 open reading frames (ORFs), from C9L to K5L, which led to limited replication in mammalian cell lines. Reinsertion of the deleted region almost completely restores its capacity to replicate in mammalian cells. However, reinsertion of the host-range genes K1L and C7L does not have the same effect, indicating the presence of additional host-range genes in the deleted region. In fact, C12L and C16L genes have been recently described as host-range genes. Several preclinical studies in different animal models have shown that DIs-based recombinant viruses expressing heterologous antigens from simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), HIV-1, SARS-CoV or SARS-CoV-2 among others, induce antigen-specific humoral and cellular immune responses while maintaining its safety profile.

KVAC103 is a new third-generation vaccine derived from the vaccine Lancy-Vaxina Berna after 103 passages in Vero cells. In vivo, KVAC103 has proven to be safe, with no symptoms of neurovirulence compared to parental or WR strains. This attenuated phenotype might be due to two major deletions in the parental strain, resulting in twenty-three deleted and four truncated genes. Recently, a KVAC103-based vaccine candidate against anthrax and smallpox expressing one of the major components of anthrax toxin (protective antigen, PA), termed KVAC103-thPA, induced binding and neutralizing antibodies against PA in mouse models. Moreover, co-immunization with KVAC103 expressing IL-15 or the immunoadjuvant cholera toxin subunit A1 (CTA1) enhanced the immune response to protective levels after a challenge with Bacillus anthracis spores. KVAC103 is a new promising third-generation vaccine candidate against smallpox and other infectious diseases; however, further research is needed to unravel its full potential.
Fourth-generation vaccines

In contrast to the classical attenuation, fourth-generation vaccines were developed by site-directed deletion or interruption of selected genes into the VACV genome. Among them we can highlight New York vaccinia virus (NYVAC), non-replicating vaccinia virus TianTan (NTV) or the recently developed Sementis Copenhagen Vector (SCV).

NYVAC is one of the best characterized genetically attenuated strains of VACV. It derives from a plaque isolate (VC-2) of the Copenhagen strain (VACV-COP) through the specific deletion of 18 ORFs: from C7L to K1L, J2R, B13R, B14R, A26L, A56R and I4L. Due to the deletion of the host-range region (from C7L to K1L), NYVAC is highly attenuated in most mammalian cell lines, including human cells, in which is unable to produce several late viral proteins due to a block in translation. However, it expresses high levels of the heterologous antigen and induces antigen-specific immune responses. For this, NYVAC is an optimal expression vector to be used as a viral-based vaccine candidate against a variety of infectious diseases. NYVAC has not been tested against smallpox, but human clinical trials with NYVAC-based vaccine candidates have shown a good safety profile and a high level of immunogenicity against different antigens, especially from HIV-1.

Another VACV attenuated strain generated through the deletion of specific genes is NTV, derived from VACV TianTan strain. NTV has been genetically attenuated through the deletion of 21,243 nucleotides, comprising 26 host-range and virulence VACV genes. This region includes the fragment from C7L to K1L genes, which makes NTV unable to replicate in most human cell lines, while maintaining replication competency in CEF cells. The replication deficiency of NTV is due to a translation shutdown of viral late protein synthesis. Preclinical studies in mice using NTV-based recombinant viruses have shown good safety and immunogenicity profiles.

SCV is a replication-defective virus generated by targeted deletion of the viral assembly gene D13L on the VACV Copenhagen strain. D13L is essential for viral replication and hence recombinant SCV vectors need to be produced on modified Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells expressing D13 and the host-range protein CP77. The vector has proven to be fully attenuated in immunocompromised mice and induced robust and long-term cellular and humoral immunity in preclinical models when expressing Zika, Chikungunya or SARS-CoV-2 antigens.

Although other attenuated VACV-based vectors have been generated and successfully evaluated in animal studies (rACAM 2000DeltaE3, vNY, VACVDelta6, etc.), in the following sections we will focus on MVA- and NYVAC-based vaccine candidates which are the most widely attenuated VACV strains used in clinical phases against MPXV, emerging viruses and HIV-1.
Timeline showing the history of the development of the different poxvirus-based vaccines.
A schematic representation showing the history of the generation of the different poxvirus-based vaccines is depicted in Figure 1 .
MVA and NYVAC Poxvirus Strains as Vaccine Candidates Against Monkeypox, Emerging Viral Diseases and AIDS
MVA-based vaccine against monkeypox virus

The monkeypox virus (MPXV), the causal agent of a zoonotic disease known as monkeypox (MPOX), was first discovered in Copenhagen in 1958. It was isolated from a research center housing monkeys that have been shipped from Singapore to Denmark. The first case of animal-to-human zoonotic transmission was identified in 1970 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) (a virus classified as genetic clade I) from a child under suspicion of smallpox. Since then, although a few cases have been identified, mainly in Europe and USA, essential viral transmission has been geographically restricted to the Central African regions. However, in 2022 we faced an increase in the spread of MPOX, with many cases identified worldwide (a virus classified as genetic clade II). During the current MPOX outbreak, from January 1 2022 to May 8 2023, a total of 87,377 cases have been confirmed globally, causing 140 deaths and affecting 111 countries. Among these, the ten countries that have reported the highest number of cumulative cases are USA (30,154 confirmed cases), Brazil (10,920), Spain (7,551), France (4,146), Colombia (4,090), Mexico (4,010), Peru (3,800), the United Kingdom (UK) (3,741), Germany (3,691) and Canada (1,484). These countries concentrate approximately the 85% of the total cases reported in 2022-2023, all of them outside the African region (data published by the WHO; May 11 2023 report).

These data show the global increase in MPOX cases, which have turned on the alarms concerning its worldwide spreading, leading to the designation as Public Health Emergency of International Concern. In 2020, a mathematical modelling study comparing MPXV with VARV showed a reproduction number (R) > 1 for MPXV, already highlighting its epidemic potential. Given these facts, the current MPOX outbreak has gained clinical relevance and the priority of promoting research focused on understanding this escalation, as well as its potential treatments and prognosis, has been reinforced.

MPXV is more than 90% identical in its coding region to other OPXVs. Due to this significant homology, cross-immunity to MPXV could have been achieved as consequence of VACV vaccination against smallpox. Nonetheless, after smallpox eradication in 1980, vaccination programs ceased, which could indicate a progressive loss of immunity against zoonotic OPXVs. In addition, after sequencing of the MPXV isolated from the 2022 MPOX outbreak, several novel mutations have been identified in comparison to its closest variant. The mutation rate of this virus seems to be higher than that generally defined for OPXVs, which could mean the accumulation of adaptative mutations that can increase its pathogenicity and transmissibility between humans. Moreover, there are many animal species that are capable of transmitting the disease to humans, thereby acting as potential reservoirs and impeding eradication. Therefore, the requirement for new and more effective vaccines against MPXV and other emerging OPXVs is on the rise.

In a study published in 1988, it was already proposed that individuals vaccinated against smallpox were resistant to MPXV infection. Ongoing concern about the 2022 MPOX outbreak has re-opened this issue and several studies support the potential utility of VACV-based vaccines in achieving MPXV immunity. Indeed, recent reports confirmed that human antibodies produced after VACV exposure cross-neutralize several OPXVs, including MPXV. Sequence analysis of MPXV isolated in the 2022 outbreak postulates that it should be recognized by the immune response induced by VACV, including the current available third-generation MVA-BN (brand names: IMVANEX in the European Union (EU), IMVAMUNE in Canada and JYNNEOS in the USA) and ACAM2000 vaccines. In addition, many preclinical studies have been developed in different animal models supporting VACV efficacy to induce MPXV immunity, especially the MVA platform. For example, it has been reported that mice vaccinated with two doses of MVA were protected against MPXV challenge, overcoming some of the contraindications observed in mice treated with Dryvax, the first-generation vaccine previously used for smallpox eradication. These results were confirmed in non-human primates (NHPs), which were also protected against MPXV challenge after immunization with the MVA-BN vaccine. In NHP models, it was also confirmed that MVA-based vaccines could induce similar or higher immunogenicity than vaccine candidates previously used for smallpox. Additionally, it has been reported that an MVA-based vaccine candidate against HIV-1 can cross-immunize against MPXV, conferring protection against a lethal MPXV challenge. VACV-based vaccines are currently being used for the development of vaccine candidates against different emerging viral diseases, including COVID-19, thus the possibility of inducing this cross-immunity could be highly valuable against new emerging orthopoxvirus infections.

As mentioned above, the substantial improvements of the third-generation VACV vaccines have allowed their clinical evaluation. The case of IMVAMUNE, an MVA-based smallpox vaccine, is especially noteworthy. This vaccine has been tested in individuals with clinical contraindications to smallpox vaccines (e.g., immunosuppressed people or people affected by skin diseases) and its safety and immunogenicity profiles have been confirmed in different clinical trials. In fact, IMVAMUNE has been approved for use in smallpox emergencies by the US Strategic National Stockpile and the EU. In 2017, IMVAMUNE administration to healthcare workers directly exposed to MPXV in the DRC was approved after noticing that primary personal equipment protection might not be sufficient to prevent viral infection. Serological analysis showed that IMVAMUNE vaccination generates significant levels of NAbs against MPXV and other OPXVs. These results have been confirmed in another clinical trial with an alternative patients' cohort and different vaccination regimens. Indeed, recent studies postulated that the effectiveness of JYNNEOS vaccination to prevent MPXV infection in different cohorts was estimated around 80%. In addition, due to the long incubation period of OPXVs, according to the US CDC, administration of the vaccine within four days of exposure may protect against MPXV infection. In an attempt to control the 2022 MPOX outbreak, different governments and regulatory agencies have approved the administration of MVA-based smallpox vaccines to healthcare workers who are directly exposed to this pathogen; as of May 2022, USA, Germany and UK support this vaccine distribution policy. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) in Europe and USA and Canada have already authorized the use of MVA-BN as vaccine against MPXV..

Although the use of MVA-BN has demonstrated substantial benefits for the prevention of MPOX, the development of more effective vaccines based on fourth-generation VACV strains and covering the newer MPXV mutations could be highly valuable against future MPOX outbreaks.
MVA and NYVAC poxvirus strains as vaccine candidates against emerging viral diseases

Given the considerable number of potential pathogens worldwide and the limited availability of resources for disease research and development (R&D), the WHO has prioritized a list of diseases and pathogens for R&D in specific contexts of public health emergencies (https://www.who.int). Currently, the priority diseases are the following: COVID-19, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), Ebola and Marburg virus diseases, Lassa fever, MERS and SARS, Nipah and other henipaviral diseases, Rift Valley fever and Zika.

In view of this global situation, in this section we review the evaluation of the most widely used third-generation MVA and fourth-generation NYVAC vectors as vaccine candidates against the emerging viral diseases prioritized by the WHO and listed above.
MVA-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2

At the end of December 2019, a new emerging coronavirus appeared causing a dramatic pandemic, currently ongoing, which affects the entire human population. Since then, the novel severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), the causative agent of the coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) pandemic, has infected more than 766 million people and caused 6.94 million deaths worldwide (https://covid19.who.int/).

Several COVID-19 vaccines have subsequently been developed showing overall good safety, immunogenicity and efficacy profiles in an extensive number of preclinical and clinical trials. COVID-19 vaccine candidates include a large variety of platforms, such as DNA and mRNA, protein subunit, inactivated and live attenuated virus and viral vector vaccines (see https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/draft-landscape-of-covid-19-candidate-vaccines for an updated list of vaccine candidates). Most of these vaccine candidates include as the main immunogen the SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein, the major structural viral protein that binds to the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) host cell receptor, allowing the attachment and infection of target cells. The most advanced vaccines (mRNA-, adenovirus vector- and protein-based vaccines) were approved by the corresponding regulatory agencies (such as the EMA in Europe and the FDA in USA) and have been administered continuously among the human population since December 2020 and early 2021, contributing to control the disease and reducing the incidence of the virus, the hospitalizations and the mortality rates.

A large number of MVA-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2 have been developed worldwide by various research laboratories and pharmaceutical companies, showing robust SARS-CoV-2-specific humoral and cellular immune responses and full efficacy against SARS-CoV-2 infection in several preclinical animal models, including mice, hamsters and NHPs. A summary of the different MVA-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2, and the main immunogenicity and efficacy results obtained when testing them in animal models is shown in Table 1 .

SARS-CoV-2 full-length S protein is the most common antigen expressed by the different MVA vectors, either in its unmodified native non-stabilized conformation or in an optimized prefusion-stabilized conformation, being the MVA vectors expressing the prefusion-stabilized S protein more immunogenic and efficacious than those expressing the non-stabilized S protein. Other regions of the SARS-CoV-2 S protein have also been inserted into the MVA vector, such as the receptor binding domain (RBD), the S1 region or a soluble S ectodomain, but their immunogenicity is lower than that induced by MVA vectors expressing the full-length S protein. Furthermore, other SARS-CoV-2 antigens, such as the N protein, have been incorporated in combination with the S protein to broaden the immune response against SARS-CoV-2. Most vaccine candidates contain the sequence of the ancestral Wuhan strain, but a synthetic MVA vector expressing SARS-CoV-2 S and N antigens from variant of concern (VoC) beta has been recently reported.

Most MVA-based vaccine candidates used the wild-type MVA strain as parental vector, but other MVA vectors have also been used, such as a synthetic MVA or a MVA vector with the immunomodulatory MVA C6L, K7R and A46R genes deleted.

The immunogenicity and efficacy of all these MVA-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2 have been assessed in preclinical studies in three main animal models: mice (BALB/c, C57BL/6 and transgenic K18-hACE2), hamsters (Syrian golden hamster) and NHPs (rhesus macaque or African green monkey) (see Table 1). Importantly, all vaccine candidates were safe and well-tolerated in animal models, with no serious adverse effects reported. In wild-type BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice, which are not susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection, SARS-CoV-2-specific humoral and cellular immune responses were mainly evaluated, while in transgenic K18-hACE2 mice, which express the human ACE2 receptor and thus are susceptible to a lethal SARS-CoV-2 challenge, the protective efficacy against SARS-CoV-2 infection was primarily tested. Hamsters and NHPs are also susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection, but unlike K18-hACE2 mice, the virus does not produce a lethal infection. Most vaccine candidates have been administered intramuscularly using either a single-dose regimen or a double-dose schedule using prime/boost immunization protocols, with doses ranging from 1 x 105 to 5 x 108 plaque-forming units (PFU) per animal. Another important route of administration is the intranasal route, which has been demonstrated to be more immunogenic than the intramuscular route, being able to induce systemic and mucosal immune responses with higher levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies (IgG, IgA and NAbs) and T cells, as well as better protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection. Other routes of administration included intraperitoneal, subcutaneous, sublingual, buccal and skin scarification routes, or combinations of intramuscular and intranasal routes. Two doses are more immunogenic and effective than one dose but, in particular, a single dose of vaccine candidates expressing a prefusion-stabilized S protein is sufficient to confer protection.

Regarding immunogenicity, binding IgG antibodies against S, RBD and/or N antigens were induced, with higher titers of IgG2c or IgG2a subtypes over IgG1, indicating a Th1-biased immune response. Moreover, NAbs against the ancestral Wuhan strain or recognizing different VoCs (alpha, beta, gamma, delta or omicron) were elicited. Some studies have also described the activation of non-neutralizing polyfunctional antibody responses with important activities, such as antibody-dependent neutrophil phagocytosis (ADNP), antibody-dependent complement deposition (ADCD), antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) and antibody-dependent natural killer activation (ADNKA). On the other hand, robust and polyfunctional SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4 and CD8 T cell responses have also been induced by most vaccine candidates, with predominance of antigen-specific CD8 T cells secreting Th1 cytokines (i.e., IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha and/or IL-2) and absence of a Th2 response. Activation of other T cell populations, such as CD4+ T follicular helper cells, CD4+ T regulatory cells or CD8+ T resident memory cells, has also been reported. Most of the studies focused on the analysis of SARS-CoV-2-specific acute immune responses, but some studies also demonstrated that long-term humoral and cellular responses are induced, at least 6-8 months post-immunization. Overall, the different MVA-based vaccine candidates have been demonstrated to be highly immunogenic in the three main animal models used, with the induction of robust SARS-CoV-2-specific humoral and cellular immune responses.

Concerning efficacy, in general terms, the different MVA-based vaccine candidates have been revealed to be highly efficacious with full protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection (mainly against the ancestral Wuhan strain) in the three main animal models tested. In the lethal K18-hACE2 mouse model, vaccinated mice challenged with SARS-CoV-2 were protected from body weight loss and mortality caused by the virus. In hamsters, SARS-CoV-2 is not lethal, but control of body weight loss was also observed in vaccinated animals, whereas in the NHP model SARS-CoV-2 infection does not induce body weight loss or mortality. The evaluation of the protection exerted showed that most of the MVA-based vaccine candidates induced a significant reduction in the levels of genomic and subgenomic SARS-CoV-2 RNA in the lower (lung) and upper (throat or nasal cavity) respiratory tracts, but with better control of SARS-CoV-2 replication in the lungs than in the upper respiratory tracts, indicating that a sterilizing immunity was not fully obtained. However, infectious viruses were undetectable in the lungs and upper respiratory tracts of the majority of vaccinated animals, demonstrating the potent efficacy of these vaccine candidates. Additionally, lung histopathology was halted in animals vaccinated, as evidenced by significant reductions in gross pathology scores, with less severe or absent manifestations of hemorrhage, atypical pneumocyte hyperplasia and vasculitis compared to control animals. Moreover, some vaccine candidates also significantly reduced the levels of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines in lungs and serum, indicating that these vaccine candidates successfully control the cytokine storm triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Importantly, it has been recently reported that the MVA-CoV2-S vaccine candidate, expressing a full-length non-stabilized S protein (Wuhan strain), completely protects K18-hACE2 mice from SARS-CoV-2 brain infection and damage. Notably, some of the vaccine candidates were also able to fully protect against a SARS-CoV-2 reinfection when inoculated several weeks to months after the first challenge or induce long-term protection up to 6 to 8 months after the last immunization. Recently, it has been reported that vaccine candidates expressing S and N proteins from Wuhan or VoC beta protect against SARS-CoV-2 challenge with Wuhan or VoCs beta and delta, confirming their capacity to control infection of several SARS-CoV-2 VoCs.

In addition, some MVA-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2 have entered human clinical trials. A phase I clinical trial (NCT04639466) was initiated in December 2020 in USA in healthy adults, using a novel synthetic MVA vector co-expressing SARS-CoV-2 S (in a non-stabilized version) and N proteins (termed COH04S1) and the results of safety and immunogenicity confirmed that the vaccine is safe and immunogenic, inducing SARS-CoV-2-specific humoral and cellular responses. Moreover, COH04S1 also induced potent and cross-reactive S- and N-specific T cell immune responses against the ancestral Wuhan strain and major VoCs. COH04S1 is currently being evaluated in phase II clinical trials in patients with blood cancer who have received cellular therapy or a stem cell transplant (NCT04977024) and as a booster dose in previously vaccinated healthy people (NCT04639466). Another MVA vaccine candidate has also entered human clinical trials in Germany. In September 2020, a phase I clinical trial (NCT04569383) was initiated with an MVA vector expressing a full-length non-stabilized S protein (MVA-SARS-2-S) but was discontinued in January 2021 due to poor immunogenicity in volunteers, despite a good safety profile. Consequently, a new MVA vector expressing a prefusion-stabilized S protein (MVA-SARS-2-ST) was generated and is currently being tested in two phase I clinical trials (NCT04895449 and NCT05226390), although no results have been published to date. One of the studies (NCT04895449) will evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of MVA-SARS-2-ST in seronegative (two single injections) and in previously vaccinated individuals (one single injection). The second study (NCT05226390) will evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of MVA-SARS-2-ST when administered as a single inhalable booster dose in 30 volunteers previously immunized with an authorized SARS-CoV-2 vaccine.

The results from all these clinical trials will be important to decipher which type of MVA-based vaccine could induce higher levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific humoral and cellular immune responses and protection against infection, and in determining which is the contribution of the MVA vector (either a synthetic MVA or a wild-type MVA) or the inserted SARS-CoV-2 antigens (S versus S and N). Future head-to-head comparative studies with different MVA-based vaccine candidates will be needed to answer these questions.

In the last years, several outbreaks of emerging or re-emerging viral diseases have occurred worldwide. This phenomenon can be attributed to several factors, such as changes in the world population (growth, density, aging, migration to urban areas or widespread travel), land use and environmental changes (deforestation, urbanization or climate change). All these factors can affect the geographic distribution of viruses, leading to increased human contact with potential zoonotic reservoirs and facilitating the transmission among the human population. Preclinical evaluation of MVA-based vaccine candidates against the high-priority emerging viral diseases prioritized by the WHO is summarized in Table 2 .

CCHF is transmitted by ticks, has a high case fatality rate (10%-40%) and is endemic in all of Africa, the Middle East, the Balkans and Asia. There are no vaccines available for animal or human use. An MVA-based vaccine candidate expressing the viral glycoprotein (GP) from CCHF virus (CCHFV) has been reported to induce humoral and cellular immunogenicity and protect mice from a lethal challenge.

According to WHO data, Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a severe, often fatal, disease that affects humans and other primates. The average case fatality rate is around 50%. The 2013-2014 outbreak in West Africa was the largest and most complex EVD outbreak since Ebola virus (EBOV) was discovered in 1976. It reached several countries, starting in Guinea and then crossing to Sierra Leone and Liberia. The immunogenicity and efficacy of MVA-based vaccine candidates against EBOV have been assessed in preclinical studies mainly in three animal models: mice (IFNAR-/-, BALB/c and C57BL/6), guinea pigs and NHPs (rhesus macaques). All vaccine candidates were safe and well-tolerated, induced humoral and cellular immunity and protected animals against EBOV infection. It is important to highlight the use of multivalent virus-like particles (VLPs) vaccines including antigens from various filoviral species, which opens the possibility of further investigation for a pan-EBOV vaccine.

In response to the 2013-2014 EVD outbreak, EBOVAC1, EBOVAC2 and EBOVAC3 clinical trials were funded by the Innovative Medicines Initiative (IMI) Ebola+ programme (https://www.ebovac.org/project-governance/), aimed to evaluate the safety, tolerability and immunogenicity of the two-dose vaccine regimen Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo. Ad26.ZEBOV is an adenovirus type 26 vector-based vaccine encoding Zaire EBOV GP (Mayinga variant), and MVA-BN-Filo is a vector encoding multivalent GPs from Zaire EBOV Mayinga variant, Sudan EBOV Gulu variant and Marburg virus Musoke variant and the nucleoprotein from Tai Forest EBOV. In May 2020, the EMA recommended granting marketing authorization for a 2-component vaccine, Zabdeno-and-Mvabea, for people aged 1 year and older. This vaccine is administered in 2 doses: first, Zabdeno (Ad26.ZEBOV) and, 8 weeks later, Mvabea (MVA-BN-Filo). This prophylactic 2-dose vaccine regimen is therefore not suitable in the case of an outbreak where immediate protection is required. The different prophylactic clinical trials using Ad- or MVA-based vaccine candidates against EBOV are summarized in Table 3 . All vaccination regimens were safe and well-tolerated. Heterologous combination using MVA as a booster was the best regimen inducing EBOV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cell responses. In addition, the magnitude and durability of the humoral immune responses were enhanced by increasing the interval between prime and boost doses. To date there are no published data on the efficacy of these vaccines in phase III clinical trials.

Marburg virus (MARV) causes the Marburg virus disease (MVD), which is clinically similar to EVD, showing a case fatality rate of up to 88%. The largest recorded outbreak of MVD occurred in Angola in 2004, but a recent outbreak was reported in Ghana in 2022. Currently, there is no approved treatment or vaccine for MVD. Preclinical data revealed that the recombinant MVA-MARV-VLP vector expressing the viral GP and VP40 proteins induced humoral and cellular immunity and protected guinea pigs from infection. An MVA-based T cell vaccine against EBOV has also been reported to protect mice against a lethal MARV challenge.

Lassa fever is endemic in Ghana, Benin, Liberia, Guinea, Mali, Togo, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, but probably also exists in other West African countries. The overall case fatality rate is 1%. Currently, no licensed vaccine for Lassa fever is available, but different potential vaccine candidates are being developed. In mice and guinea pigs a single dose of MVA-based vectors expressing different LASV antigens protected animals against a LASV challenge.
Prophylactic clinical trials using MVA-MERS-S as a vaccine candidate against MERS-CoV.

Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) was first identified in Saudi Arabia in 2012. It is a zoonotic virus transferred to humans from infected camels and dromedaries and human-to-human transmission is also possible. MERS has a case fatality rate of 34.4%. MERS outbreaks occurred in Saudi Arabia in 2014 and in South Korea in 2015. Although transmission is predominantly detected in the Arabian Peninsula, there is a significant risk of exporting cases outside the Middle East as a result of travelling. Therefore, it is necessary to halt this transmission and control potential future outbreaks. In this context, the development of vaccine candidates against MERS-CoV has been challenging because the correlates of protection remain poorly understood and the reduced number of cases made the design of efficacy clinical trials difficult. Thus, no specific vaccine or treatment against MERS-CoV is currently available, although several products are under development. Different studies have reported the preclinical and clinical evaluation of MVA-based vaccine candidates targeting the MERS-CoV spike (S) glycoprotein. In animal models (mice and camels) MVA-MERS-S induced high levels of NAbs with capacity to reduce the transmission of the virus to humans. The vector was also evaluated as prophylactic vaccine in clinical trials (Table 4 ), demonstrating safety and tolerability profiles and eliciting specific long-term antibodies and B cell immunity.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is a viral respiratory disease caused by SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV). It was first identified in 2003 during an outbreak in China. The case fatality rate is around 3%, and it was the first severe and transmissible new disease to arise in the 21st century, showing an evident capacity to spread along international air travel routes. There is no cure or vaccine for SARS. Several preclinical studies in different animal models have evaluated the immunogenicity induced by different MVA-based vaccine candidates expressing spike or nucleocapsid proteins from SARS-CoV, demonstrating high levels of specific NAbs as well as strong humoral and cellular immune responses at systemic and mucosal levels.

Nipah virus (NiV) infection is a zoonotic illness that can also be directly transmitted from person-to-person or through contaminated food. The case fatality rate is estimated to be between 40% and 75%. Several outbreaks have occurred in Malaysia, India and Bangladesh. Currently, no drugs or vaccines to treat or cure NiV infection are available. The epitopes responsible for NiV glycoprotein G-specific immune responses have been characterized using the vaccine candidate MVA-NiV-G. A soluble NiV-G version was beneficial in activating NiV-G-specific cellular responses using these peptides.

Rift Valley fever (RVF) is a viral zoonosis that primarily affects animals, but it also has the ability to infect humans. It was first identified in Kenya and since then different outbreaks have been reported in North and sub-Saharan Africa. In 2000, RVF cases were reported in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. An inactivated vaccine has been produced for human use; however, although it has been experimentally used to protect laboratory and veterinary personnel at high risk of RVF exposure, it is not licensed or commercially available. Other vaccine candidates are currently being investigated. The immunogenicity and efficacy of different MVA-based vaccine candidates against RVF virus (RVFV) targeting the GP GnGc protein have been evaluated in different animal models, achieving partial protection.

Finally, Zika virus (ZIKV) is mainly transmitted by the bite of an infected mosquito, from mother to fetus during pregnancy or through blood and blood products transfusions, sexual contact and organ transplantation. ZIKV disease cases have decreased globally since 2017, but virus transmission persists at low levels in several countries in the Americas and other endemic regions. To date, 89 countries and regions have reported evidence of mosquito-borne ZIKV infection. No vaccine is available for the prevention or treatment of ZIKV infection. However, promising results are derived from preclinical studies in mice using MVA-based vaccine candidates expressing ZIKV antigens. It has been reported the induction of potent and polyfunctional ZIKV-specific CD8 T cell responses, that mainly exhibited an effector memory phenotype, using an MVA-based vector expressing ZIKV prM and E structural proteins (MVA-ZIKV). In addition, an alternative MVA-based vector expressing ZIKV non-structural protein 1 (NS1) (MVA-ZIKV-NS1) induced potent humoral and cellular immune responses and fully protected mice against a lethal intracerebral ZIKV challenge, preventing the potential risk of Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE) associated with the use of ZIKV vaccines expressing structural proteins.
Clinical applications of attenuated MVA and NYVAC poxvirus strains as vaccine candidates against HIV-1

In 2021, 1.5 million people were newly infected with HIV-1, 38.4 million people were living with HIV-1 and 650,000 people died of AIDS-related illnesses (https://www.unaids.org/en). The development of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-1 patients and its application as preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to contribute to prevent infection of high-risk individuals has been an important step forward in the HIV-1 field; however, it does not replace the urgent need for an effective vaccine. Given that developing countries comprise approximately 90% of people living with HIV-1 and ART is inaccessible, it is clear that an effective vaccine is needed to halt transmission and eliminate HIV-1.

While different HIV-1 vaccine regimens have been evaluated in clinical trials following three main approaches (induction of NAbs, induction of CD8+ T cells and heterologous prime-boost regimens to elicit both humoral and cellular responses), only eight HIV-1 efficacy trials have been conducted to date. Among them, the RV144 phase III clinical trial in Thailand was the only one that showed some efficacy (31.2%) against HIV-1 infection in healthy individuals primed with ALVAC-HIV vCP1521 (an attenuated avipoxvirus-based vector) and boosted with AIDSVAX B/E protein at 42 months post-vaccination. In this RV144 trial, binding IgG antibodies against conserved regions of the V1/V2 loop, binding IgG3 antibody responses to gp120 Env protein and antibodies mediating antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) in the presence of low plasma IgA levels correlated with a reduced risk of HIV-1 infection.
Prophylactic clinical trials using the MVA vector as a vaccine candidate against HIV-1.

RV144 trial reinforced the use of attenuated poxviruses as vaccine candidates against HIV-1. In this context, prophylactic and therapeutic clinical trials reported in the last eight years using MVA or NYVAC vectors expressing different HIV-1 antigens are summarized in Table 5, Table 6, Table 7 . Previous clinical trials are reviewed in Sanchez-Sampedro et al. MVA- and NYVAC-based vaccine candidates evaluated in different immunization regimens have been reported to be safe, well-tolerated and capable of inducing HIV-1-specific potent, polyfunctional and durable T cell responses, as well as HIV-1-specific binding and neutralizing antibodies in various degrees.
Genetic Optimization of Attenuated MVA and NYVAC Poxvirus Strains

Despite the great safety and immunogenicity profiles demonstrated by MVA- and NYVAC-based recombinant vectors, there is a continuous effort to develop novel and optimized vaccine candidates able to induce stronger, broader and longer-lasting immune responses to heterologous antigens. Thus, several genetic modifications have been implemented in order to enhance the immunogenicity and efficacy of these vaccine candidates, such as the deletion of immunomodulatory genes, the insertion of host-range genes and the enhancement of the viral promoter strength.

One of the most commonly used strategies to enhance host immune responses to vaccination with poxvirus-based vaccine candidates is the deletion of specific viral genes that are involved in the modulation of the host immunity. The genes that have been deleted in MVA and NYVAC genomes can be categorized based on the function of their protein products in: Interferon (IFN) inhibitors (B8R, B19R, C6L and N2L), soluble cytokine inhibitors (A41L, B7R, B16R and C12L), TLR signalling inhibitors (A46R, A52R, B15R and K7R), virulence factors (A40R) and unknown non-essential genes (B6R, B9R and B10R). This deletion strategy has been used in the development of MVA- and NYVAC-based recombinant viruses as vaccine candidates against HIV-1. The outcomes of preclinical studies conducted in mice and NHPs are summarized in Table 8 .

The deletion of poxvirus immunomodulatory genes results in enhanced immune responses to heterologous antigens. However, increasing the number of genes deleted does not always guarantee a more robust immune response due to the complex and unpredictable nature of virus-host interactions. Despite this issue, the combined deletion of selected immunomodulatory genes remains a viable strategy for the development of novel and optimized poxviral vaccine candidates.

Based on these results, MVA-based vectors lacking the viral immunosuppressive genes C6L, K7R and A46R and expressing SARS-CoV-2, ZIKV or EBOV antigens have been generated, inducing potent antigen-specific B and T cell responses in immunized mice and conferring protection against a challenge with the corresponding virus in susceptible mouse models.
Insertion of host-range genes

With the insertion of lacking or orthologous host-range genes, attenuated vectors such as MVA or NYVAC are able to recover the ability to replicate in human cells, increasing not only the activation of specific host cell signalling pathways but also the timing and expression level of the heterologous antigen, which promote an enhanced activation of immune responses, maintaining a highly attenuated phenotype. This strategy has primarily been used for the generation of poxvirus-based vaccine candidates against HIV-1.

Reinsertion of the host-range gene C7L into a NYVAC-based vaccine candidate against HIV-1 enhanced the expression of HIV-1 antigens in vitro and increased the magnitude of HIV-1-specific T cell responses in mice. Reinsertion of both C7L and K1L host-range genes into NYVAC genome resulted in enhanced expression of HIV-1 antigens in vitro, activation of pathways involved in antigen processing and presentation, enhanced cross-presentation to HIV-1-specific CD8 T cells and proliferation of HIV-1-specific memory CD8 T cells in vitro, together with induction of HIV-1-specific CD4 and CD8 T cell immune responses, high levels of anti-Env binding antibodies, enhanced ADCC responses and neutralizing capacity in rhesus monkeys, concomitantly with low levels of IgA antibodies. Reinsertion of B13R host-range gene into an MVA-based vaccine candidate against HIV-1 induced an apoptosis delay in different cellular types including antigen-presenting cells in vitro and an enhancement of HIV-1-specific humoral responses in mice.
Enhancement of the viral promoter strength

The recognition of a specific antigen by the immune system is influenced by how efficiently the antigen is processed and presented on the surface of infected cells. In this context, the timing of heterologous antigen expression from MVA or NYVAC vectors under the control of a VACV promoter influences the type, quantity, quality and durability of antigen-specific responses and results crucial to induce robust antigen-specific T cell responses. It has also been reported that the expression levels of heterologous antigens correlate with the magnitude of antigen-specific immune responses in mice. Therefore, the optimization of the viral promoter strength is an effective strategy to increase both the timing and the expression levels of heterologous antigens. Traditionally, VACV promoters with early and/or late functions have been used to drive the expression of heterologous antigens; however, novel strong VACV promoters have been recently designed through different approaches, such as the use of tandem promoters naturally present in VACV genome, the generation of hybrid early-late synthetic promoters, the in silico design of novel promoters based on early and late consensus motifs present in native poxvirus promoters or the engineering of potent new promoters using bioinformatic analysis. Among them, the synthetic early/late promoter (sE/L) and the Late/Early Optimized promoter (LEO160) are particularly interesting.

The sE/L promoter is a 40-bp synthetic VACV promoter that contains largely overlapping early and late regulatory elements. It has been reported to induce higher early and total expression levels of the heterologous antigen compared to other VACV promoters, including the extensively used P7.5 early/late promoter. This sE/L promoter has been widely used in the generation of MVA- and NYVAC-based vaccine candidates against SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV/SARS-CoV, EBOV/MARV and HIV-1. The LEO160 promoter was designed using bioinformatic tools and generated by swapping the early and late elements of the sE/L promoter with a modification in the spacer region between the early element and the transcriptional start site. The LEO promoter enhanced green fluorescent protein (GFP) and HIV-1 gp120 expression in vitro and the magnitude of HIV-1 gp120-specific B and T cells responses in mice. Moreover, this novel promoter has been recently used in the generation of an MVA-based vaccine candidate against ZIKV that achieved full protection in challenged mice.
Concluding Remarks and Future Prospects

Studies on the poxvirus family have provided major breakthroughs in science. In fact, the first human viral vaccine was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796 against smallpox, and this medical treatment opened a new era in vaccinology. Moreover, new discoveries about the mode of poxvirus entry, transcription, translation, DNA replication, assembly and virus release were seminal in the understanding of virus biology, pathogenesis and behaviour of cells during virus-host cell interactions, and also opened new paths in the field of immunology. Hence, in this review we describe the evolution of poxvirus-based vaccines, from first-generation to current status, pointing out the main strategies that have been followed up to optimize the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy of attenuated poxvirus strains and their contribution as vaccine vectors against emerging viral diseases with pandemic potential. Based on the current status of the scientific knowledge provided on poxvirus vaccines, we highlight some future prospects.

Although many preclinical and clinical studies have been conducted with poxvirus vectors, both against viral infectious diseases and tumors, to date only two MVA-based vaccines have been approved for human use by the FDA and the EMA. MVA-BN-Filo has been approved against EBOV as a component of a prime/boost combination with Ad26.ZEBOV, while MVA-BN has been approved against VARV and MPXV. Why are not there more poxvirus-based vaccines for human use? This is probably related to the occasional adverse effects that were observed with the initial first- and second-generation poxvirus-based vaccines in humans, but this limitation was overcome with the use of highly attenuated third- and fourth-generation vectors, such as MVA and NYVAC, respectively. Considering the multiple studies performed with poxvirus vectors and their good behavior as vaccines, efforts should be done to increase the number of approved vaccines.

What are the advantages and disadvantages in the use of highly attenuated poxviruses as vaccine vectors? These vectors have the added benefit of being non-replicative in human cells, display a high safety profile, can incorporate multiple genes of interest in their DNA genome and are able to induce potent and long-term humoral and cellular specific immune responses with high protective efficacy against infection. In addition, the immune response elicited against the vector itself using replication incompetent vectors is reduced, compared to replication-competent poxvirus-based vectors, and the same vector (i.e., MVA and NYVAC) can be used in repeated boosters without loss of triggering immune responses to the heterologous antigen. This represents a favorable scenario for vaccination against another pathogen using the same poxvirus vector but expressing a different foreign antigen. In fact, immunization protocols including repeated vaccinations with the same poxvirus vector have been evaluated in clinical trials, triggering significant levels of specific long-term immune responses. The use of two doses of attenuated poxvirus vectors in a homologous prime/boost vaccination protocol is a common practice generally applied in preclinical and clinical studies. What are the disadvantages? One drawback is that the highly attenuated poxvirus vectors do not grow to similar levels as the replication-competent vectors. This has been highlighted during the MPOX epidemic, where the only approved vaccine (MVA-BN; IMVANEX/IMVAMUNE/JYNNEOS) could not be delivered as requested by the affected countries due to limitations on the vaccine production. Thus, strategies to improve virus growth should be assessed. One of these strategies involves the reinsertion of host-range genes within the viral genome of non-replicating vectors in human cells, where the ability of the virus to grow to higher yields was recovered. Another apparent disadvantage of poxviruses as vaccine vectors is the large number of viral proteins that are produced during infection that interfere with the immunogenicity induced by the heterologous antigen. However, this effect could be compensated through the activation of an immune response broader than that obtained using a single immunogen (i.e., protein, DNA, mRNA). In addition, the prolonged immune response elicited by replication-competent vectors, a distinguishing feature of classical smallpox vaccines, could become an advantage in order to maintain durable long-term B cell immune responses with minimal vaccine doses. Moreover, different technologies in the use and manipulation of poxviruses for vaccine purposes have been recently applied, such as the incorporation of the CRISPR/Cas9 approach for the rapid generation of viral recombinants or the reconstitution of synthetic viral genomes, innovative procedures accelerating the practical application of these DNA viruses.

Another future prospect is the use of poxvirus-based vectors in combination with other vaccines. While recombinant poxviruses have been shown to be efficient inducers of antigen-specific B and T cell responses when combined in heterologous prime/boost immunization protocols with other vaccine platforms (i.e., DNA, mRNA, protein subunits, adenovirus, influenza virus and VSV), being preferable the administration of the poxvirus vector as a booster, it will be relevant to determine the immunological differences in the innate, acute and memory B and T cell responses between poxvirus vaccine platform and other platforms when compared head-to-head in homologous versus heterologous combinations. This is an area of research in which we need to know the impact, at molecular and cellular levels, of a poxvirus vaccine on the immune system, from the initial antigen delivery administered by different routes (i.e., scarification, intradermal, intramuscular and intranasal), to short to long times after vaccine administration. There are still questions to be addressed on the mode of action of distinct vaccine platforms, e.g., on how an mRNA, viral vector or subunit protein vaccine compares/differs from a poxvirus-based vector vaccine. Since poxvirus vectors are potent inducers of antigen-specific CD8 T cells, unidirectional targeting of this type of T cells, directed either to infected or tumor cells, will contribute to eliminate more effectively infectious agents and cancer cells. The control of highly pathogenic emerging viruses and tumors should be explored with optimized poxvirus vectors inducing potent and durable antigen-specific CD8 T cell responses, which could be generated using the different approaches highlighted in this review.

There are lessons to be learned in the development of vaccines against novel pathogens. During the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, the public was in general skeptical about how quickly, one year, vaccines were developed, but this was because industry and the scientific community with years of experience in the development of vaccines against viral diseases were prepared to respond promptly when SARS-CoV-2 emerged at the end of 2019, and the sequence was published in January 2020. Undoubtedly, the appearance of the COVID-19 pandemic and other emerging viral diseases outlined by WHO, together with current uncertainties on whether an H5N1 flu human pandemic could occur, has made the field of virology essential for providing advanced knowledge to be prepared to control emerging viruses. This preparedness was rapidly implemented when MPXV appeared in May 2022, simply because an effective MVA-based vaccine against MPXV was developed years before. The contribution of virologists against the COVID-19 pandemic was highly recognized by society, from the development of vaccine candidates to the understanding on how a virus infects the host cell and the mechanisms of virus replication, transmission, evolution and pathogenesis. Virologists, along with other scientists and clinicians, were acclaimed for their achievements in the control of the SARS-CoV-2 infection, contributing to reduce hospitalizations and deaths. Overall, this review will help scientists from different disciplines to better understand vaccine advances in the poxvirus field and how this knowledge may benefit other areas of science.

passages.text: Is Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Always a Familial and Inherited Disease?

Virtually since its inception, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) has been regarded as a genetically transmitted disease, often demonstrating an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, and supported by the monogenic sarcomere mutation hypothesis. This construct has been promoted universally for HCM with respect to both disease cause and transmission of clinically overt phenotype within families. The principle that HCM can occur in families and be responsible for heart failure disability or arrhythmic sudden death often serves as a source of both anxiety and guilt on the part of families.

However, it has been our experience that many families with HCM may not demonstrate an autosomal dominant pattern of transmission. Notably, the concept of a nonfamilial form of HCM first emerged in the 1960s, and was more recently revisited by Ingles et al in 2017 when the authors reported 40% of families as having nonfamilial HCM, based on absent HCM family history and without a sarcomeric mutation on genetic testing in the proband. Nonfamilial HCM was associated with benign clinical course, although this study did not evaluate HCM phenotypes in all relatives.

With these considerations in mind, we embarked on a systematic analysis in 2022 at the Lahey HCM Center interrogating 304 consecutive families to determine whether there was evidence of inherited HCM. Each family surveyed included a referred patient (representing the proband) in whom an HCM diagnosis was confirmed at our center. Data that support the findings of this study are available from the authors on reasonable request. The study was reviewed and approved by Institutional Review Board at Lahey Hospital and Medical Center, allowing retrospective review of medical records and granted a waiver of informed consent in accord with 45 CFR 164.512(i)2(ii).

This analysis of 304 families with HCM identified 130 (43%) with some evidence of a genetic disease (ie, either a relative or a proband with a pathogenic/likely pathogenic HCM sarcomere mutation [n=55], >=1 relative of any degree with known or probable HCM phenotype [n=53], or both [n=22]).

In addition, 163 other families could not be judged reliably as having either familial or nonfamilial HCM because of a variety of indicators: insufficient compliance or impractical logistics for acquiring comprehensive family information; offspring in last generation aged <18 years or a noninformative small pedigree; or sudden death in young relatives with or without HCM confirmation.

Ultimately, we were able to identify 11 individual families (4% of 304), all composed of 3 generations, who met our predefined criterion of nonfamilial disease (ie, absence of the HCM phenotype in first-degree relatives by echocardiography and/or cardiac magnetic resonance, clinical events, or other evidence of HCM) (Figure). Also, in the extended family beyond first-degree relatives, no patient had a personal history consistent with HCM. Because of the self-imposed restrictions in our conservative study design, we have likely underestimated nonfamilial HCM in our study population.
Four study pedigrees demonstrating the nonfamilial form of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).
Clear symbols indicate absence of evidence of HCM; solid symbols, clinically confirmed HCM; and symbols with slash, died of non-HCM disease. Subject ages are in parentheses. Arrows indicate probands.

The 11 pedigrees consisted of 7 relatives on average (range, 5-8), aged 57+-19 years. The 11 probands were aged 45 to 77 years (mean+-SD, 62+-10 years); 73% were men; left ventricular thickness was 17+-2 mm; and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (gradient >=30 mm Hg) occurred in 64%, including 5 with surgical septal myectomy.

For molecular genetic testing, a commercial panel of 30 genes associated with HCM and its most common phenocopies was used: ACTC1, ACTN2, ALPK3, ANKRD1, CSRP3, FHL1, FLNC, GLA, JPH2, LAMP2, MYBPC3, MYH6, MYH7, MYL2, MYL3, MYPN, NEXN, PLN, PRKAG2, PTPN11, RAF1, RIT1, SOS1, TCAP, TNNC1, TNNI3, TNNT2, TPM1, TTR, and VCL. No pathogenic/likely pathogenic mutations or variants of uncertain significance were identified in any probands or relatives.

Our novel data from Lahey HCM Center suggest that not all families with HCM demonstrate autosomal dominance, and by inference HCM may not be a familial or inherited disease in all cases. This demonstration of sarcomere-negative and nonfamilial HCM pedigrees is an important observation from a scientific perspective, as it may relate directly to the fundamental basis of HCM. In addition, there are important clinical inferences from our findings for families. Recognizing that evidence for an autosomal dominant disease may not be apparent in all families is highly relevant given that this patient population deserves a realistic understanding of the risk (or lack thereof) for transmitting their clinical disease to offspring or others, a concern that is often unavoidably associated with substantial anxiety. We also acknowledge that pedigree size and other competing factors could be relevant to our conclusions about penetrance and lack of familial inheritance.

Therefore, in conclusion, our identification of novel documentation of individual pedigrees with nonfamilial HCM is highly relevant to the overriding principle that patients with HCM deserve access to the most relevant clinical information about their complex heterogeneous disease, including the possibility that this disease may not be transmitted to other family members.

passages.text: Potential of macronutrients and probiotics to boost immunity in patients with SARS-COV-2: a narrative review

Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-COV-2) may cause inflammation and increased cytokine secretion. Dietary factors may play an important role in enhancing the immune responses against infectious diseases such as SARS-COV-2. This narrative review aims to determine the effectiveness of macronutrients and probiotics to improve immunity in SARS-COV-2 patients. Dietary proteins may boost pulmonary function in SARS-COV-2 patients through inhibitory effects on the Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and reduce Angiotensin (ANG-II). Moreover, omega-3 fatty acids may improve oxygenation, acidosis, and renal function. Dietary fiber may also produce anti-inflammatory effects by reducing the level of high-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP), Interleukin (IL-6), and Tumor necrosis factor (TNF-alpha). In addition, some evidence indicates that probiotics significantly improve oxygen saturation which may enhance survival rate. In conclusion, the consumption of a healthy diet including adequate macronutrients and probiotic intake may decrease inflammation and oxidative stress. Following this dietary practice is likely to strengthen the immune system and have beneficial effects against SARS-COV-2.
Introduction

Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-COV-2) is a viral infectious disease that in the previous 2 years has caused a worldwide pandemic. In December 2019 (Wuhan, China) SARS-COV-2 was first reported and characterized as a pandemic in March 2020 by the World Health Organization (WHO). Millions of people worldwide have been infected with SARS-COV-2, while over six million people have died from this disease. The symptoms of COVID-19 vary from asymptomatic to mild upper respiratory tract symptoms and can progress to pneumonia. Patients with severe pneumonia rapidly deteriorate over a short period and require advanced medical support. SARS-COV-2 colonizes the respiratory tract but can also invade the gastrointestinal tract, neurological system, kidneys, and other organs. SARS-COV-2 utilizes the host cell membrane receptor ACE2 to enter the virus into lymphocytes, monocytes, pulmonary alveoli, and esophageal epithelial cells. The cytokine storm can be induced by increases in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha, in which a hyperactive immune response is experienced. The effects of this response include vessel and lung alveoli damage, and systemic organ failure, such as acute respiratory syndrome (ARDS), which has been associated with high rates of mortality.

Immunity to viruses can be influenced by several factors such as genetics, vaccination history, illness, medications, sex, stage of life (e.g., pregnancy, infancy, and old age), and diet. Specifically, an adequate intake of some dietary components is essential for developing, supplying, and expressing immune responses. A balanced diet of macronutrients (i.e., carbohydrates, protein, and fats) has anti-inflammatory effects and can affect different stages of the immune response. Consequently, an unbalanced diet of macronutrients can affect innate and adaptive immunity, hence making people more susceptible to infections and severe clinical conditions.

Recent studies reported that critically ill patients with SARS-COV-2 are at high risk for malnutrition. In this context, a recent study emphasized the supportive role of dietary supplementation in SARS-COV-2 patients. Therefore, following a well-balanced diet in combination with certain dietary supplements may strengthen and optimise the function of the immune system. Particular types of supplements shown to have antiviral activities against common respiratory viruses are probiotics. These dietary supplements can regulate cytokine secretion and affect the immune response. At present there is limited evidence on macronutrients and probiotics intake in patients with SARS-COV-2. The aim of this narrative review was to examine the effects of macronutrients and probiotics on the immune system in patients with SARS-COV-2.
Protein

Proteins are essential to life because they facilitate biochemical reactions and enzyme production. They also act as cellular signals in the form of hormones and cytokines. An adequate protein intake is necessary for antibody production in the body. An adult requires 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight to meet the recommended dietary allowance (RDA). Key amino acids for stimulating the immune system include arginine and glutamine. Arginine serves as the vital substrate for synthesizing nitric oxide by macrophages and endows them with pro-inflammatory and microbicidal properties. As for glutamine, this amino acid is used as an energy source for the immune cells similar to glucose.
The immunomodulatory role of protein in SARS-COV-2

To defeat the barrier and bind the host cells in the alveoli, SARS-COV-2 utilizes ACE2 (membrane-bound enzyme localized on type II pneumocystis) and cellular serine protease transmembrane protease, serine 2 (TMPRSS2) to prime and replicate in infected organisms. ACE2 is expressed in endothelial cells including the heart, kidneys, and intestines. When the SARS-COV-2 has entered ACE2-positive cells, there is a down-regulation of the enzyme. ACE2 usually binds angiotensin II, a molecule recently certified as a critical player in the conventional renin-angiotensin system (RAS) which promotes inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis. The pro-inflammatory angiotensin II is converted into the anti-inflammatory angiotensin 1-7 by binding the enzyme to angiotensin receptors, which exerts a pro-inflammatory effect. Therefore, higher production of angiotensin 1-7 can protect the endothelial barriers of the lungs, kidneys, heart, and intestines supporting patients with viral respiratory tract infections from harmful inflammation. Dietary peptides with inhibitory effects on the angiotensin-converting-I enzyme (ACE-I) can significantly reduce angiotensin (ANG-II). Dietary-derived peptides can contribute to the downstream ANG-II function. The lactoferrin-released tetra-peptide RPYL (62% of concentration 300 mumol/l) has been found to have inhibitory effects on ANG-II vasoconstriction. Additionally, lysine has been found to down-regulate the level of ANG-II.

Asymptomatic and mild SARS-COV-2 patients treated with lactoferrin (a milk-derived 80-kDa glycoprotein) had faster clinical recovery compared to untreated patients. Therefore, lactoferrin (Lf) may be a safe treatment combined with other therapies for COVID-19 patients. A retrospective study focused on the antiviral activity of Lf found that SARS-CoV-2 RNA was negativized faster in Lf treated versus untreated patients.

Evidence from previous review studies indicates that a diet that positively impacts immune function contains adequate amounts of protein, particularly glutamine, arginine, and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). Dietary intake of anserine, carnosine, and 4-hydroxyproline has been shown to improve the body's immunological defenses against bacteria, fungi, parasites, and viruses. Soy protein enhances cellular immunity through a reduction in TNF-alpha concentrations. However, primary sources of amino acids include fish, meat, and poultry. Therefore ensuring that the intake of peptides is optimised may improve respiratory function, symptoms, and fatigue in SARS-COV-2 patients. Support for this recommendation is shown by impaired immunity with protein-deficient diets, which would increase the risk of COVID-19 infection (Figure 1).
